opus-5.5.text:
Evolution has been running the largest experiment imaginable for about four billion years. Every genome alive today is a record of what worked: the variants that survived selection. Most mutations that broke something essential got filtered out. So when you look across millions of genomes, you're really looking at the results of trillions of experiments, and the patterns of what's conserved, what varies, and what co-varies tell you a lot about function.

The idea with Evo is that if you train a model to predict the next base pair in DNA, the only way to get really good at that is to internalize the rules that produced those sequences. Language models learned grammar, facts, and some reasoning just from predicting the next word. We're betting the same thing happens in biology. To predict DNA well, the model has to implicitly learn what makes a protein fold, which mutations are tolerated, how regulatory elements are arranged, and how genes in an operon or a CRISPR system work together.

What makes DNA especially interesting is that it's the most fundamental layer. Protein language models have been powerful, but proteins are only part of the story. DNA also encodes RNA, regulation, and how genes are organized. By working at single-nucleotide resolution with very long context, Evo can see across those layers at once, so it can learn about protein–RNA interactions or whole multi-gene systems rather than one molecule at a time.

That has practical payoffs. Without being explicitly trained for it, the model can score mutations for fitness effects zero-shot, because evolution already taught it which changes are deleterious. And because it's generative, you can sample new sequences, like new CRISPR systems or other functional elements, and some of them actually work when you test them in the lab.

So I think of it as moving biology from a descriptive science, where we catalog what nature made, toward one where we can learn the underlying design principles and then write new sequences ourselves. Evolution generated the training data; our job is to build models that can read it and, eventually, write in that language too.

r001.rationale: The response says next-base prediction teaches Evo which mutations are tolerated and lets it score mutations for fitness effects, including identifying deleterious changes. This clearly links sequence prediction to distinguishing variants by their functional effects.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that evolution has been running this enormous experiment for billions of years. It generates variation, and natural selection filters that variation through the question of whether an organism can survive and reproduce. The sequences we observe today are a record of that process. We don’t get to see every failed experiment, but we do get to see what persisted.

With Evo, we train a model to predict the next nucleotide in a DNA sequence. That sounds like a very simple task. But to do it well across many different organisms, the model has to learn some of the constraints that make biology work. A nucleotide isn’t independent of everything around it. It can be part of a protein-coding gene, a regulatory element, or an RNA structure, and its role can depend on sequences much farther away.

So the hypothesis is that, by learning to predict sequences at scale, the model learns something about the biological relationships that produced them—even though we haven’t explicitly labeled all those relationships. And then we can ask whether that knowledge transfers: Can it help predict the effect of a mutation? Can it generate a new sequence that actually functions?

That last step is crucial. A sequence that looks plausible to a model isn’t necessarily functional. Evolution gives us this extraordinary training dataset, but experiments are how we find out what the model has really learned.

r001.rationale: The response says next-nucleotide prediction may teach biological constraints and asks whether that knowledge can help predict mutation effects. It does not clearly explain that this prediction captures distinctions between variants with different functional effects.

sol-6.1.text:
Evolution has been running this enormous experiment for billions of years. It generates variation, and then selection filters that variation through the constraints of survival and reproduction. The sequences we observe today are a record of that process.

With Evo, we train a model to predict the next piece of DNA given the sequence that comes before it. That sounds like a simple task, but to do it well across many different genomes, the model has to learn something about the underlying biology: what makes a gene work, how genes are organized, and how different parts of a sequence depend on one another.

The exciting possibility is that prediction becomes a way to learn those constraints without explicitly specifying every rule. Then we can ask whether the model can use what it has learned to predict the effects of mutations or generate new sequences with useful functions. Of course, evolution’s record isn’t a controlled experiment, so experimental validation is essential. But it gives us an extraordinary amount of biological information to learn from.

r001.rationale: The response says next-sequence prediction may help predict mutation effects, but does not explain that it captures distinctions between variants with different effects on biological function.
